description: Display types, screen sizes, RAM vs storage, and processing power — how hardware shapes HCI design.
hero_image_caption: A range of digital devices showing different screen sizes and display technologies.
content_html:
Why Hardware Shapes Interface Design

Every HCI — whether it is a banking app on a phone, a self-checkout screen at a supermarket, or a fitness tracker on your wrist — runs on real hardware. The hardware choices available to a designer directly affect what the interface can look, feel and do. In the exam, questions on this topic often ask you to select suitable hardware for a given scenario or explain the impact of a hardware constraint on interface design. This lesson gives you the vocabulary and reasoning to answer those questions confidently.

Display Type

The type of display screen shapes what an HCI can show and how users interact with it. The four main display types are LCD (Liquid Crystal Display), OLED (Organic Light-Emitting Diode), e-ink, and capacitive touchscreen.

LCD screens are cost-effective and widely used on laptops, desktop monitors and retail tills. They require a backlight, which makes them less energy-efficient than OLED but suitable when cost matters. OLED screens produce richer colours and deeper blacks because each pixel lights itself. This makes them ideal for premium smartphone and TV interfaces where visual quality drives the user experience. E-ink screens use almost no power and are easy to read in bright sunlight — making them ideal for e-readers and bus-stop information displays that need long battery life and outdoor readability. Capacitive touchscreens allow finger-based interaction and are embedded in smartphones, self-service kiosks and point-of-sale terminals. The interface design must account for this: buttons need to be large enough to tap accurately, and hover states used on desktop menus become irrelevant.

Display Size

Screen size directly determines how much information can fit on the display at once and how the interface is laid out. A smartwatch screen (typically 1–2 inches) can display only a few lines of text or a single metric at a time — its HCI must use large icons, simple swipe gestures and minimal text. A smartphone screen (typically 5–7 inches) supports richer layouts but designers still favour mobile-first principles: large tap targets, scrollable content and simplified navigation. A laptop or desktop screen (13–34 inches) allows multi-column layouts, dense menus and complex dashboards that would be unreadable on smaller screens. A smartboard (interactive whiteboard, 55–86 inches) is designed for group use from a distance — text must be large enough to read across a classroom, and the interface should support large gestures rather than precise taps.

Key Fact

Display type and size together shape the entire HCI layout. A small OLED touchscreen (smartwatch) forces minimal-text, icon-based design; a large non-touch LCD monitor allows dense multi-column layouts. Matching display choice to context is a core design decision.

Memory (RAM) vs Storage — A Critical Distinction

This distinction is explicitly flagged in examiner reports as a source of lost marks. Many students confuse memory and storage, or use the two words interchangeably. They are different.

RAM (Random Access Memory) is temporary. It holds whatever the processor is actively working with at this moment — the running app, the open browser tabs, the data being processed. When you switch the device off, RAM is wiped completely. More RAM means the device can keep more things open and running simultaneously without slowing down. For HCI design, insufficient RAM means sluggish animations, delayed responses when typing, and apps crashing when multitasking. A banking app with smooth transitions and real-time balance updates needs sufficient RAM to function as designed.

Storage (on a hard drive, SSD or flash memory) is permanent. It holds files, apps and the operating system even when the device is switched off. More storage means more apps and files can be saved on the device. For HCI design, storage capacity affects how many features an app can install locally versus requiring an internet connection to stream. It does not affect the speed of the running interface directly — that is RAM’s role.

The examiner report is explicit: many students write about “memory” when they mean storage, and vice versa. A question such as “Explain how RAM affects the performance of an HCI” requires you to say that RAM is temporary working memory for actively running processes, and that insufficient RAM causes slowdowns and crashes during use. Saying “more memory means more files can be saved” scores zero — that describes storage, not RAM.

Use this quick test: if data disappears when you turn the device off, it is RAM. If data is still there after switching off and on, it is storage. The exam will give you a scenario (e.g. a self-service kiosk) and ask you to explain the impact of RAM or storage — apply this distinction directly to the scenario.

Key Fact

RAM is temporary working memory — it holds actively running data and is wiped on shutdown. Storage is permanent — it holds files and apps between sessions. RAM affects interface speed and responsiveness; storage affects how much can be saved locally on the device.

Processing Power

The processor (CPU) executes the instructions that make an HCI function. Processing power determines how quickly the device can carry out calculations, render graphics and respond to user input. An interface that runs on a low-powered processor — such as an embedded system in a washing machine — must be simple and lightweight: minimal graphics, no animations, limited options. A high-powered desktop processor can run complex data dashboards with real-time charts, animated transitions and multiple simultaneous background processes.

When a question gives you a scenario — “a hospital reception kiosk” or “a portable stock-checking device for a warehouse” — work through each hardware consideration in turn. For display: what screen size does the context require? Does the user interact by touch or indirectly? For RAM: does the HCI need to keep multiple processes running at once, or is it a single-purpose tool? For storage: does it need to store data locally, or does it connect to a network database? For processing power: does the interface need real-time updates, animations or heavy calculations?

A hospital reception kiosk might need a large capacitive touchscreen (accessible to users of varying abilities), moderate RAM (running a booking system and checking in patients simultaneously) and modest local storage (it connects to the hospital’s main server rather than storing records locally). A wearable fitness tracker needs a small OLED touchscreen, minimal RAM (it only tracks one or two metrics) and very low processing power — because everything must fit within a tiny battery budget.
exam_tip_html: The most common error on hardware questions is confusing RAM with storage. Remember: RAM is temporary and affects speed while the device is running; storage is permanent and affects how much can be saved. If a question uses the command word “explain”, you must link the hardware consideration to its specific impact on the HCI — for example, “insufficient RAM will cause the animation to lag because the processor cannot hold all the required data in working memory simultaneously.” Naming the hardware feature without explaining the impact scores only partial marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Display type (LCD, OLED, e-ink, capacitive touchscreen) and size (smartwatch to smartboard) directly shape what an HCI can show and how users interact with it — the designer must match both to the context.
  • RAM is temporary working memory that affects interface speed and responsiveness; storage is permanent and affects how much data and how many apps the device can hold. These are different things and must not be confused in the exam.
  • Processing power determines how complex and responsive an HCI can be — low-powered devices need simple, lightweight interfaces; powerful devices can support rich animations, real-time data and multiple simultaneous features.

practice_questions.text: Which display type uses almost no power and is highly readable in direct sunlight, making it suitable for outdoor information screens?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: e-ink (only). Distractors: LCD (requires backlight, less readable in sunlight), OLED (power-hungry per pixel, reflective in bright light), capacitive touchscreen (a touch input method, not a display technology in the same sense).

practice_questions.text: State one difference between RAM and storage.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: accept any one accurate contrast, e.g. RAM is temporary (wiped when the device powers off) whereas storage is permanent (data remains after shutdown) (1); OR RAM holds actively running data whereas storage holds saved files and installed applications (1); OR RAM affects processing speed and responsiveness whereas storage determines how much data can be saved (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline how display size affects the design of an HCI for a smartwatch compared with a desktop monitor.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: smartwatch screens are very small (1–2 inches) so the HCI must use large icons, minimal text and simple gestures because little content fits on screen at once (1); desktop monitor screens are large (13–34 inches) and support multi-column layouts, dense menus and detailed dashboards because much more content can be shown simultaneously (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how insufficient RAM affects the user experience of an HCI. Give an example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: RAM holds the data and instructions being actively processed by the device; if there is insufficient RAM, the processor cannot hold all required data in working memory simultaneously (1), causing the HCI to slow down, animations to stutter or apps to crash — for example, a banking app with multiple open tabs and real-time balance updates may freeze if the device runs out of RAM (1). Award 1 mark for correctly identifying RAM as working/temporary memory without linking to the user experience impact.

practice_questions.text: Explain how processing power affects the design decisions a developer makes when creating an HCI for an embedded system in a domestic appliance compared with a financial trading dashboard.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): identifies that embedded systems in domestic appliances have low processing power, so the HCI must be simple and lightweight — minimal graphics, few options, no animations — because the processor cannot execute complex instructions quickly (1); a financial trading dashboard runs on a high-powered desktop system and can therefore support real-time charts, animated data visualisations and multiple simultaneous background processes (1); concludes that processing power directly constrains design complexity — the designer must not include features the available processor cannot execute within an acceptable response time (1).
Secure (2): two of the three mark points developed; link between processing power and design decisions partially explained.
Developing (1): states that more processing power enables a 'better' interface without explaining the specific design consequences.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: A designer is creating an HCI for a self-service checkout terminal in a supermarket. The terminal uses a capacitive touchscreen and must process transactions, display product information and manage a receipt printer simultaneously. Sketch a comparison of the hardware considerations for this terminal versus a wearable fitness tracker. In your sketch, address display type, display size, RAM and processing power for each device. Justify each hardware choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): sketch or structured response clearly addresses all four hardware considerations for both devices (1 per consideration per device = up to 8, capped at 8). For the self-service terminal: large capacitive touchscreen (accessible touch interaction for diverse users, transaction input) (1); large display (55+ cm, product images visible from normal standing distance) (1); sufficient RAM to run payment processing, product database queries and peripheral control simultaneously without lag (1); adequate processing power for real-time transaction handling and fast UI responses to prevent queue build-up (1). For the fitness tracker: small OLED or LCD touchscreen (compact, visible in varied lighting, low profile on wrist) (1); small display (2–3 cm, shows only key metrics: steps, heart rate) (1); minimal RAM (single-purpose device, tracks one or two data streams) (1); low processing power (battery life is the priority; complex calculations are sent to the paired smartphone) (1). Accept reasonable alternative justified choices.
Secure (5–6): most considerations addressed for both devices with clear justification; one or two gaps.
Developing (3–4): addresses hardware for one device in depth or covers all four considerations without justification.
Emerging (1–2): names hardware components with no contextual justification.
0: no creditworthy content.

knowledge_checks.q: What happens to data stored in RAM when a device is switched off?
options: It is copied to the hard drive
It is permanently deleted and cannot be recovered
It is wiped — RAM is temporary and holds only actively used data

knowledge_checks.q: Which display type is most suitable for an outdoor bus-stop information screen that needs to run for long periods without recharging?
_____ is temporary working memory that holds actively running apps and data, and is wiped when the device is powered off.
An HCI on a smartwatch must use large icons and minimal text because the _____ is very small, limiting how much content can be displayed at once.
Match each hardware consideration to its impact on HCI design.
right: Determines how complex and responsive the interface can be
Affects how much content fits on screen and how the layout is structured
Controls how fast the device responds and whether animations run smoothly during use
Affects whether touch interaction is possible and how visible the screen is in different lighting

flashcard_questions.a: Temporary working memory that holds actively running data; wiped when device powers off.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between RAM and storage?
flashcard_questions.a: RAM is temporary (holds running data); storage is permanent (holds saved files and apps).

flashcard_questions.q: What display type is best for outdoor low-power screens?
flashcard_questions.a: E-ink — it reflects ambient light and uses almost no power.
A display where each pixel generates its own light, giving deeper blacks and better contrast than LCD.

flashcard_questions.q: How does low RAM affect an HCI?
flashcard_questions.a: Causes slowdowns, stuttering animations and app crashes during use.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must a smartwatch HCI use large icons and minimal text?
flashcard_questions.a: Because the display is very small (1–2 inches), limiting how much content fits on screen.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a capacitive touchscreen enable in HCI design?
flashcard_questions.a: Direct finger interaction — buttons replace menus; hover states are removed.

flashcard_questions.q: How does processing power affect HCI complexity?
flashcard_questions.a: Low-powered devices need simple, lightweight interfaces; powerful devices support real-time data and animations.

flashcard_questions.q: What does storage affect in an HCI context?
flashcard_questions.a: How many apps and files can be saved locally on the device.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the four main display types in this unit.

glossary_terms.definition: Liquid Crystal Display — a screen that uses a backlight shining through a grid of liquid crystals to produce images; found on most budget monitors and laptops.
Organic Light-Emitting Diode — a screen where each pixel generates its own light, giving deeper blacks, better contrast and thinner panels than LCD.
Electronic ink — a low-power display that reflects ambient light rather than emitting it, used in e-readers; highly readable in sunlight but cannot display fast movement.
A touch-sensitive LCD or OLED screen that detects finger pressure or electrical charge, enabling direct interaction without a separate input device.
Temporary, fast storage that holds the data and programs actively being used by the processor right now; it is wiped when the device is switched off.
